explanation_or_combination: Hb ↓ + Ferritinë ↓
source_ref: J. Snook, N. Bhala, I. L. P. Beales, et al., "British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines for the management of iron deficiency anaemia in adults," *Gut*, vol. 70, no. 11, pp. 2030–2051, 2021, doi: 10.1136/gutjnl-2021-324757. https://gut.bmj.com/content/70/11/2030
evidence: Anaemia = Hb below the lower limit of normal for the population; "Serum ferritin is the single most useful marker of IDA … <15 µg/L indicative of absent iron stores, <30 µg/L generally indicative of low body iron stores."
note: SUPPORTED; Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: a normal/high ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency in inflammation. The rule fires only on low ferritin, which is the specific direction.

explanation_or_combination: Hb ↓ + MCV ↓
source_ref: H. S. Chaudhry and M. R. Kasarla, "Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia," in *StatPearls* [Internet], Treasure Island, FL: StatPearls Publishing, updated Feb. 2026. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470252/
evidence: Microcytic anaemia = "low MCV (RBC volume <80 fL) and low hemoglobin content"; iron deficiency is "the most common cause", then thalassaemia, lead poisoning.
note: SUPPORTED; Textbook (NCBI Bookshelf), not a society guideline. Back-up (opened): M. W. Short and J. E. Domagalski, "Iron Deficiency Anemia: Evaluation and Management," *Am Fam Physician*, vol. 87, no. 2, pp. 98–104, 2013, https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2013/0115/p98.html. Combination points to a differential (iron deficiency, thalassaemia, ACD, sideroblastic), not one diagnosis.

explanation_or_combination: Hb ↓ + Vitaminë B12 ↓
source_ref: R. C. Langan and A. J. Goodbred, "Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Recognition and Management," *American Family Physician*, vol. 96, no. 6, pp. 384–389, 2017. https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2017/0915/p384.html
evidence: "Vitamin B12 deficiency is a common cause of megaloblastic anemia"; evaluation = CBC + serum B12; "<150 pg per mL (111 pmol per L) is diagnostic for deficiency."
note: SUPPORTED; Classic picture also has MCV ↑ (macrocytic). BSH 2014 (Devalia et al., *Br J Haematol* 166:496–513) and NICE NG239 returned 403 — cite only if you open them yourself. Folate deficiency must be excluded.

explanation_or_combination: Glukozë ↑ + HbA1c ↑
source_ref: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee, "2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025," *Diabetes Care*, vol. 48, suppl. 1, pp. S27–S49, 2025, doi: 10.2337/dc25-S002. https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/48/Supplement_1/S27/157566
evidence: Thresholds A1C ≥6.5 %, FPG ≥126 mg/dL, 2-h/random PG ≥200 mg/dL; "In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests which may be obtained at the same time (e.g., A1C and FPG)".
note: SUPPORTED; Strongest of the 11: ADA names the glucose + A1C pair explicitly. Keep the rule as "warrants evaluation" (fasting state, NGSP assay, haemoglobinopathies affect A1C).

explanation_or_combination: Kreatininë ↑ + Ure ↑
source_ref: A. O. Hosten, "BUN and Creatinine," in *Clinical Methods: The History, Physical, and Laboratory Examinations*, 3rd ed., H. K. Walker, W. D. Hall, J. W. Hurst, Eds. Boston, MA: Butterworths, 1990, ch. 193. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK305/
evidence: "The BUN and sCr are screening tests of renal function … they essentially reflect GFR"; values stay normal until >50 % of renal function is lost; a disproportionately high BUN should prompt a search for extrarenal (prerenal/postrenal) factors.
note: SUPPORTED; KDIGO 2024 (403, not opened) stages CKD on eGFR, not urea, so a textbook azotaemia reference is the right source for a urea+creatinine pair. Textbook is from 1990 — standard but old; say so. Urea is non-specific (dehydration, GI bleed, protein intake, steroids).

explanation_or_combination: ALT ↑ + AST ↑
source_ref: P. N. Newsome, R. Cramb, S. M. Davison, et al., "Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests," *Gut*, vol. 67, no. 1, pp. 6–19, 2018, doi: 10.1136/gutjnl-2017-315541. https://gut.bmj.com/content/67/1/6
evidence: "AST and ALT are enzymes present in hepatocytes and are released into the blood stream in response to hepatocyte injury or death (hepatitis)"; "Hepatitic—predominantly raised ALT and AST indicate hepatocellular liver injury".
note: SUPPORTED; BSG guideline, open access. AST also of muscle/cardiac origin; AST:ALT ratio and magnitude matter.

explanation_or_combination: ALP ↑ + GGT ↑
source_ref: Same as P06 (Newsome et al., *Gut* 2018;67(1):6–19). https://gut.bmj.com/content/67/1/6
evidence: "Cholestatic—predominantly raised ALP and GGT indicate cholestasis"; GGT "can be useful in confirming that an elevated ALP is of liver and not bony origin".
note: SUPPORTED; Guideline frames GGT exactly as the discriminator for a raised ALP. GGT alone is non-specific (alcohol, drugs, obesity).

explanation_or_combination: TSH ↑ + fT4 ↓
source_ref: S. A. Wilson, L. A. Stem, and R. D. Bruehlman, "Hypothyroidism: Diagnosis and Treatment," *American Family Physician*, vol. 103, no. 10, pp. 605–613, 2021. https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0515/p605.html
evidence: "If the TSH level is high (greater than 4.5 mIU per L), a serum FT4 level should be obtained. A low FT4 level indicates clinical hypothyroidism … An FT4 level within the reference range indicates subclinical hypothyroidism."
note: SUPPORTED; NICE NG145 and Jonklaas 2014 (ATA) could not be opened (403/CAPTCHA); the ATA document is a treatment guideline without the biochemical definition. Applies to primary (not central) hypothyroidism.

explanation_or_combination: TSH ↓ + fT4 ↑
source_ref: D. S. Ross, H. B. Burch, D. S. Cooper, et al., "2016 American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis," *Thyroid*, vol. 26, no. 10, pp. 1343–1421, 2016, doi: 10.1089/thy.2016.0229. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/thy.2016.0229
evidence: "In overt hyperthyroidism, serum free T4, T3, or both are elevated, and serum TSH is subnormal (usually <0.01 mU/L …)"; subclinical = normal fT4/T3 with subnormal TSH.
note: SUPPORTED; Back-up (opened): I. Kravets, "Hyperthyroidism: Diagnosis and Treatment," *Am Fam Physician*, vol. 93, no. 5, pp. 363–370, 2016, https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2016/0301/p363.html. T3-toxicosis (low TSH, normal fT4) is not captured by the rule.

explanation_or_combination: Leukocite ↑ + CRP ↑
source_ref: L. K. Riley and J. Rupert, "Evaluation of Patients with Leukocytosis," *American Family Physician*, vol. 92, no. 11, pp. 1004–1011, 2015. https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2015/1201/p1004.html
evidence: "Leukocytosis is one of the hallmarks of infection"; Table 3 under Infection: "Consider use of other biomarkers, such as CRP and procalcitonin"; under Chronic inflammation: "Consider erythrocyte sedimentation rate and CRP levels".
note: **PARTIAL**; No guideline formally defines a WBC+CRP pair; the review links leukocytosis to infection/inflammation and names CRP as the complementary marker — that is the honest extent. CRP support (opened): A. Markanday, "Acute Phase Reactants in Infections," *Open Forum Infect Dis*, vol. 2, no. 3, ofv098, 2015, doi: 10.1093/ofid/ofv098. Both markers non-specific (surgery, trauma, steroids, smoking, malignancy). Consider dropping or keeping with this caveat.

explanation_or_combination: LDL ↑ + HDL ↓

Catapano, et al., "2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias: lipid modification to reduce cardiovascular risk," *European Heart Journal*, vol. 41, no. 1, pp. 111–188, 2020, doi: 10.1093/eurheartj/ehz455. https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/41/1/111/5556353

note: SUPPORTED; Low HDL is a risk *marker*, not a treatment target ("no evidence from randomized trials that therapeutically increasing plasma HDL-C reduces the risk of CV events"). Rule correctly framed as cardiovascular-risk evaluation.
